title: Different answers
hookLine: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood: the traditions see work differently
carry: the part matters more than the applause
last: FULLY THERE FOR THE WARM WATER AND THE PLATE.

cards: A lunch break, and five coworkers share a bench outside. Ask each what their work really is, under the job title. The first says: it's the price of being alive.
The second: it's what I was made for. The third: I do it for someone else, not for me. The fourth: it's my part, and somebody has to do it.
The fifth shrugs: it pays the rent, and I try to earn it honestly. Nobody on that bench is wrong. Over these weeks on work, each of those answers has turned up in a tradition on this path.
Today, all five go side by side.

teach.b: First, the curse. In Genesis, outside the garden, the ground turns hard, and the King James words are blunt: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." Some readers hear a punishment there.
Others hear plain honesty: work is hard. Second, the calling.

Martin Luther taught that a milkmaid or a cobbler serving the neighbor is doing holy work, and the letter to the Colossians says: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men."
Third, the offering. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever he does, eats or gives can be done as an offering. The work goes up like a gift, and the result stops being the point.
Fourth, the duty. The Gita again: better your own duty done imperfectly than someone else's done well. Your work is your part, and the part matters more than the applause.
Fifth, livelihood. The Buddha names trades to avoid, such as dealing in weapons and poisons: earn a living in a way that doesn't harm. These aren't five rival theories where one has to win.

teach.h: AS AN OFFERING, AS A DUTY.
teach.b: The Gita itself holds two of them, offering and duty, in one book.
A nurse can call her work a calling and still feel the sweat of it after a night shift.
And the answer can change with the season of a life, or the day of the week. On a Monday it's sweat. On a good Thursday, it might be an offering.

how: People on different paths describe their work through their own tradition's lens: some as a calling, some as an offering or a duty, some as an honest livelihood, and some as simply hard and necessary.

o: the many job titles people hold across a lifetime
seeing work as curse, calling, offering, duty or livelihood
the idea that one view of work must win over the rest

games.q: five answers about work — tap the pairs.
p: whatever you do, as an offering

s: you have to pick one view of work and drop the rest
the traditions hold several at once; the Gita gives both offering and duty.
the Buddha names trades to avoid, such as dealing in weapons and poisons
earn a living in a way that doesn't harm.

Luther taught that a milkmaid's or a cobbler's work can be a holy calling.

games.q: your own work, done imperfectly, or someone else's, done well. which does the Gita say is better?
games.why: the Gita says better your own duty done imperfectly than another's done well. the part matters more than the applause.

practice: Say the five words slowly to yourself: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood. Hold your own work up to each one, the way you'd hold a shirt up in front of a mirror, and notice which fits today, maybe two at once.
If you pray, you can offer that word in your own tradition's way.

wordCard.voice: Different answers. Curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood: the traditions see work in different ways, and a person can hold more than one. Today's word.
